title: HarnessTax: Does Your Claude Need Claude Code?
html:
HarnessTax: Does Your Claude Need Claude Code?

Melissa Z. Pan1, Shuo Yang1, Negar Arabzadeh1, Wei-Lin Chiang2, Ion Stoica1, Matei Zaharia1

1 UC Berkeley · 2 Arena Intelligence Inc.

Language models are changing how we build software and solve computational problems1,2. Coding agents put these capabilities to work through harness, a software system that manages a model’s tools, context, and task execution3. While models provide the core intelligence behind coding agents, harnesses are increasingly seen as central to how effectively that intelligence is used and extracted3,4. Choosing a coding agent therefore means choosing both a model and a harness, even when the explicit focus is only on the model.

Millions of people already use coding agents. OpenAI reported more than 5 million weekly active Codex users in June 2026, and Anthropic reported that Claude Code’s weekly active users doubled in the first six weeks of 2026.5,6 Programming also accounted for more than half of OpenRouter’s token volume by late 2025.7 But the impact of harness choice remains unclear. What does the harness actually add, and at what cost?

One missing piece is understanding of how the model and harness work together. Performance reports for Anthropic models in Claude Code or GPT models in Codex tell us how each pair performs. Could the same model solve more tasks, or achieve the same success at lower cost, in another harness?

We evaluate 21 model–harness pairs spanning seven models and three harnesses—Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Pi—on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0.8,9 Our study reveals three key findings:

  1. Harness choice affects cost more than task success on the benchmarks we test. The same model can achieve similar solve rates at substantially different costs.
  2. A minimal harness can be competitive. Pi shows that a simpler, open-source harness can be competitive on both cost and task success.
  3. Models can perform competitively outside their provider’s harness. A model’s provider does not necessarily offer its most effective pairing. So it turns out that your Claude models may not need Claude Code…

We examine each finding below and will publicly release our profiling traces.

Experiment Setup

We compare 21 model–harness pairs on the same 30 randomly sampled tasks from each benchmark: SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0. We run each pair three times per task to capture variation between attempts. We use each harness’s native configuration, cap each attempt at 100 turns, and select its corresponding high effort setting. Step and effort settings follow each harness’s own definitions. We measure task success using each benchmark’s official evaluator. We access Kimi K3 via Firework AI.

Measurement details. We first average cost and success over each task’s three attempts, then average across the 30 tasks. We estimate 95% confidence intervals using 10,000 bootstrap resamples. Each resample draws 30 task averages with replacement and recomputes the overall mean. This means we resample tasks using their three-attempt averages. We compute token cost using a fixed direct-API price list dated September 1, 2026, applying the same prices to each model across harnesses.

(1/3) Harness affects cost more than correctness.

The same model often achieves a similar solve rate at substantially different costs. GPT-5.6 Luna offers the lowest cost on both benchmarks, while Claude Fable 5 reaches the highest solve rate on SWE-bench Lite. \melissa{Kimi K3: update the comparison once the new results are confirmed.} However, these models do not have substantial performance differences when changing across harnesses. Fable 5 achieves a 95.6% success rate with both Pi and Claude Code, yet Claude Code costs about twice as much per attempt: $0.87 versus $0.42. \melissa{double check number when new ones come in }

Figure 1. Token cost and success rate for 13 model–harness pairs on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0. Each marker averages 90 attempts: three attempts on each of 30 randomly sampled tasks. Colors identify models; marker shapes identify harnesses. The stepped line marks the observed Pareto frontier: no evaluated alternative improves cost or success without worsening the other. Use the model buttons to highlight a model’s results across harnesses and the harness buttons to show each harness’s Pareto frontier.

Fable 5 with Claude Code achieves best accuracy on Pareto than with Pi by 1% but at x% more cost. The cost gap extends beyond Fable 5. Across shared models, Claude Code costs about 2.0× as much as Pi and 3.1× as much as Codex on SWE-bench Lite, and 2.1× as much as Pi on Terminal-Bench 2.0, using geometric means of cost ratios. Meanwhile, the estimated harness effects on success rate remain within ±3%.}

You may be paying a hidden “harness tax” when you accept a coding agent’s default harness without comparing alternatives. Model evaluations should therefore compare the same model’s cost and task success across commonly used harnesses. Results from one harness cannot show whether another could achieve a similar solve rate for less.

(2/3) A minimal harness can be competitive.

The natural question, then, is why some harnesses are more efficient than others. We examine cumulative cost–success curves and recorded agent turn counts to investigate these differences.

Figure 2. Cumulative cost–success curves. For each model–harness pair, we sort all 90 completed rollouts by their final cost, grouping equal costs. Each point shows cumulative cost on the x-axis and cumulative successful rollouts on the y-axis, both divided by 90. Failed rollouts add cost without adding success. Curves closer to the upper-left show more cumulative success at lower cost. A nine-point moving average smooths the curves; the unsmoothed endpoint matches the pair’s mean cost and success rate in Figure 1.

Similar agent turns can lead to substantial different costs. For Fable 5 on SWE-bench Lite, Codex and Claude Code average turns differ by just about 4% (respectively 11.8 and 12.3), but Claude Code costs [confirm cost premium]% more per attempt, with a [Δ]-percentage-point difference in success rate. Such a cost gap suggests higher average spend per agent turn in Claude Code than Codex.

Pi and Codex show that open-source harnesses can be competitive on the benchmarks we test. Pi exposes just four tools by default—read, write, edit, and bash.10 Its configurations reach the Pareto frontier on both benchmarks. Codex CLI is also open-source and includes built-in planning, prompt caching, and automatic context compaction.11 Both achieve strong results with different harness designs. Claude Code’s public documentation describes richer features by default such as subagent delegation, and automatic context management.12 \melissa{Verify system-prompt lengths in the evaluated versions before making a comparative claim.} \tbd{For [model] on [benchmark], Claude Code reaches a higher final success rate at greater cost.} This does not imply that richer harness features are generally unnecessary.

Different harnesses can encourage different interaction behavior. \tbd{In our inspection of failed SWE-bench Lite runs with Haiku, we find five cases in Claude Code and one in Codex where the model stops to request further user input. In the corresponding Pi runs, the model proceeds with the same original benchmark prompts.} The benchmark provides no follow-up input, so stopping to ask a question leaves the attempt unfinished and scored as a failure. This does not establish whether the model could implement the fix with further interaction. These cases may reflect that Claude Code is designed for getting more user feedback. Thus harness’s usefulness in an interactive workflow may therefore differ from standard benchmark score.

The effectiveness of Pi and Codex demonstrates opportunities for open harness research with existing models. Researchers can work with SOTA coding harnesses without access to proprietary harnesses or co-training with the model. Richer harness features may still benefit other models, workloads, or interaction settings. Harness complexity should therefore be treated as an empirical trade-off, not an assumed advantage.1

1 *\tbd{In our evaluated configuration, Pi uses the default tools [with just X extensions to set reasoning effort for fair comparison] and reaches [success rate] at [cost] on [benchmark].}

(3/3) Models can perform competitively outside their provider’s harness.

Figure 3. Mean token cost per attempt and success rate for each model across Pi, Codex CLI, and Claude Code on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0. Whiskers show 95% confidence intervals. Green outlines identify each model’s lowest cost and highest success rate separately. The broken cost bar extends beyond the displayed axis.

Yes… you’re reading the plot correctly: Opus achieves a higher measured solve rate in Codex than in Claude Code, at less than half the cost. On our SWE-bench Lite sample, Opus 4.8 success rates 86.7% of attempts in Codex versus 83.3% in Claude Code, at $0.22 versus $0.49 per attempt.

The result extends beyond Opus and beyond Claude Code. Sonnet 4.6 achieves a 66.7% success rate in Codex versus 58.9% in Claude Code on SWE-bench Lite, while costing about 42% less ($0.41 versus $0.71 per attempt). GPT-5.6 Sol also performs competitively outside its provider’s harness: on Terminal-Bench 2.0, it achieves an 83.3% success rate in Pi versus 78.9% in Codex, at half the cost ($0.42 versus $0.84). Across the six Anthropic and OpenAI models and both benchmarks, an alternative harness achieves the highest observed solve rate in nine of twelve comparisons.

These results show that a model’s capabilities are compatible, generalizable and can carry over to other harnesses. Providers do report to optimize some models for their own coding environments: OpenAI, for example, describes GPT-5-Codex as optimized for agentic software engineering in Codex.13 Yet we observe that a shared provider does not guarantee the best pairing. The practical question remains which harness delivers the best balance of cost and task success for a given model and workload. And thus evaluation is required for cross harnesses and models.

Your Claude may not need Claude Code after all… 🤔

Ending Notes

HarnessTax shows that the same model can achieve similar solve rates at substantially different costs. On the benchmarks we test, minimal open-source harnesses can be competitive, and models can perform well outside their provider’s harness. Choosing a coding agent therefore also means choosing how much we pay to use a model’s capabilities. A harness tax can go unnoticed when we focus only on task success.

More broadly, the need for different harnesses depends on what is the role of coding agents. For day to day coding tasks, the role of harness serves as an efficient interface to tools, context, and execution. Additional guardrails, and features may not be necessary for many tasks. While, harder problems that are at the boundary of pushing model capability may still benefit from more structured support for exploring ideas, evaluating candidates, and learning from feedback.

HarnessTax is a step toward understanding models and harnesses jointly. The next step is to examine whether these patterns hold in real development workflows, where requirements evolve, developers provide feedback, and tasks extend across sessions. Measuring cost and task success alongside developer effort would help establish which harness features earn their cost in practice.
